questions.question_text:
The number $x=3$ is a zero of $P(x)=x^{4}-8x^{3}+18x^{2}-27$.
Which is the first derivative of $P$ that is not zero at $x=3$?

options.why: Checked only that $P(3)=0$ and assumed the very next derivative must be non-zero, but $P'(3)=108-216+108=0$.
Stopped one derivative early: $P''(3)=108-144+36=0$, so $P''$ is still zero at $x=3$.
Read a multiplicity of $3$ as meaning the first three derivatives after $P'$ all vanish, counting one derivative too far; in fact $P'''(3)=24\ne0$.

questions.question_text:
It is known that $x=-1$ is a zero of $P(x)=x^{4}-6x^{2}-8x-3$.
What is its multiplicity?

options.why: Only $P(-1)=0$ was checked; $P'(-1)$ is zero too, so the zero repeats.
Stopped at $P'(-1)=0$ without testing $P''(-1)$, which is also zero.
Used the degree of $P(x)$ rather than the order of the first non-zero derivative.

questions.question_text:
The polynomial $P(x)=x^{3}-27x-54$ has a double zero.
What is it?

options.why: Took the other zero of $P'$ without testing it in $P$; $P(3)=-108\ne0$.
Selected the remaining simple zero; $P(6)=0$ but $P'(6)=81\ne0$.
Added the two repeated zeroes, $-3+(-3)=-6$, instead of stating the repeated zero itself.

questions.question_text:
A polynomial $P(x)$ satisfies $P(-3)=0$, $P'(-3)=0$, $P''(-3)=0$ and $P'''(-3)\ne0$.
Which option gives the highest power of the factor corresponding to the zero $x=-3$?

options.why: The zero is $x=-3$, so the factor is $(x+3)$, not $(x-3)$.
Used only $P(-3)=0$ and $P'(-3)=0$ and ignored $P''(-3)=0$.
Combines both errors: the wrong sign in the factor and one derivative condition ignored.

questions.solution_text:
$P(-3)=P'(-3)=P''(-3)=0$, so $x=-3$ is a zero of multiplicity at least $3$.
$P'''(-3)\ne0$, so the multiplicity is exactly $3$.
The highest power is $(x+3)^{3}$.

questions.question_text:
The polynomial $P(x)=x^{3}-48x+128$ has a double zero.
What is it?

options.why: Took the other zero of $P'$ without testing it in $P$; $P(-4)=256\ne0$.
This is the remaining simple zero, found from the sum of the zeroes.
After obtaining $x^{2}=16$, divided $16$ by $2$ to get $8$ instead of taking its square root.

questions.question_text:
The polynomial $P(x)=x^{3}-12x^{2}+k$ has a double zero.
Find the possible values of $k$.

options.why: Sign slip in $P(8)=512-768+k$, giving $k=-256$ instead of $k=256$.
Discarded the stationary point $x=0$, which also gives a double zero when $k=0$.
Substituted $x=4$ instead of the correct stationary point $x=8$; $P(4)=64-192+k=k-128$ gives $k=128$.

questions.question_text:
The polynomial $P(x)=x^{3}+bx^{2}+cx-16$ has a double zero at $x=4$.
Find $b$ and $c$.

options.why: Sign slip when back-substituting into $4b+c=-12$.
Sign slip when solving $4b=-36$ for $b$.
Moved the constant terms without changing their signs, writing $4b+c=12$ and $8b+c=48$; subtraction then gives $b=9$ and substitution gives $c=12-36=-24$.

questions.question_text:
The polynomial $P(x)=x^{3}+px+q$, with $p\ne0$, has a double zero.
Which relationship must $p$ and $q$ satisfy?

options.why: Sign error when squaring $\alpha=-\dfrac{3q}{2p}$ and substituting into $\alpha^{2}=-\dfrac{p}{3}$.
The coefficients $4$ and $27$ have been attached to the wrong letters.
This is the condition for a double zero of a quadratic, not of this cubic.

questions.solution_text:
Let the double zero be $x=\alpha$, so $P(\alpha)=0$ and $P'(\alpha)=0$.
$P'(x)=3x^{2}+p$
$3\alpha^{2}+p=0$
$\alpha^{2}=-\dfrac{p}{3}$
$P(\alpha)=\alpha^{3}+p\alpha+q$
$=0$
$\alpha(\alpha^{2}+p)=-q$
$\alpha\left(-\dfrac{p}{3}+p\right)=-q$
$\dfrac{2p\alpha}{3}=-q$
$\alpha=-\dfrac{3q}{2p}$
$\dfrac{9q^{2}}{4p^{2}}=-\dfrac{p}{3}$
$27q^{2}=-4p^{3}$
$4p^{3}+27q^{2}=0$
